“First” refers to the beginning of the separation, and “return” to its end. The argument concerns all worlds, not only their elements. A permanent division of two bodies of the same kind—for example, two suns or two spheres—would require permanent force, but the heavens are not moved by force. They would have to return to natural unity, which would also bring the earlier contradictions. Ordinary individuals of one kind in our world are different: each individual passes away, while the kind continues only through successive individuals. The argument also rules out a world naturally made of many separate individuals from the start: their like parts would have to be separate too, yielding multiplicity without any unity.

Natural place is essential to a body of a given nature and cannot vary. If the places themselves joined together, place would have to move and have another place of its own. Nor can what is the center become an outer edge. — س قده
Such a union is possible in itself, even if the physical arrangement of the world would prevent it from actually occurring because it would require empty space or a break in the heavens. — س قده

Avicenna argues that no different natural movement or sensible quality means there can be no naturally different bodily world. One might object that the same effect can arise from different causes—for example, heat from fire, anger, movement, or the sun. The reply is that this resemblance holds only at a broad level; on closer examination, the kinds of heat differ. Even “evenness,” which applies to four, eight, and other numbers, is an abstract feature with no separate instance in them. Abstract features follow the things from which they are drawn, and one concept cannot come from wholly different things precisely as different. — س قده
The author first divides straight movement into three kinds, then revises this to a two-way division: movement either toward or away from the center.

The nineteen qualities are nine familiar simple tastes, four active and passive tangible qualities, three qualities of hearing, sight, and smell, and three qualities sensed indirectly. It would be more precise to list the basic tangible qualities individually. The author’s point is that the natural world has an ordered governance; as the active intellect governs this world in the philosophers’ account, so a governing power oversees the elemental world. — س قده

If nature moved a thing into a higher kind before completing the lower kind, there would be a sudden jump in its qualitative or substantial development. The philosophers reject such leaps, as they reject a sudden jump in place. This is the principle that a lower possibility must be fulfilled before a higher stage can be reached; it applies to the ascending order of things. — س قده
A sense and what it senses are correlatives and correspond to one another. A rational soul therefore has every sense that is fully represented in rational being.

Indirectly sensed things include quantity and relation. Avicenna names the most common and clearest examples. Geometrical body is counted among bodily qualities, and boundaries are included in shape. Movement and stillness are mentioned after movement and its divisions: stillness is the absence of movement in a place where movement is possible. They may also be counted as qualities in their own right, or as general kinds listed after their specific kinds. — س قده

The author gives an argument about the world’s unity that can speak to several philosophical approaches. His own view goes further than connection or contact: the parts of the world are genuinely one in existence, where what distinguishes them is the same reality that they share. Every earlier form is contained as potential matter within the final form of the complete human being, which gathers the forms of the world. What is indeterminate exists only through what gives it determination, so the world is fully actual through this final form, which itself exists through God. In another way, the kinds of beings are gathered into their higher principles and ultimately into the light of the human kind. The world’s cycles and changes pass, while this deeper unity remains. — س قده
The argument relies on one kind of dependence: a body causes another body only with a relation of position, and position cannot relate a body to something that does not yet exist. — س قده

An intellect must act and so would produce a bodily shadow or effect in the world; a soul must govern a body. Either way, separate intellects or souls would imply other bodies, whose existence has already been ruled out. The author sets aside the first claim because it would make the argument only persuasive, not conclusive.

Parts can be classified in four ways. They may share one external existence and be parts expressed in a definition, such as broader kind and defining feature; or be distinct parts considered in thought, like mental matter and form. Or they may have several existences: parts separated by position, such as parts of size, or external parts like real matter and form. — س قده

One might object that broader kind and defining feature are parts of what a thing is, not of its existence. The reply is that “existence” here includes the thing’s being established as real. The priority meant is priority in the thing’s basic reality, not necessarily temporal priority or efficient causation. — س قده

Parts of size may be posterior in actuality, since the mind first has a magnitude and then divides it. But magnitude itself makes division possible; that is what is meant by its parts. A point or an immaterial thing does not contain such divisible parts. Also, if a body had parts of size but no parts in its definition, it would still have matter and form, and therefore broader kind and defining feature, contrary to the premise. — س قده

The proof that dimensions cannot be infinite is this: one body cannot be the cause of another body of the same kind in a way that makes one prior to the other. If the Necessary Being were an extended body and caused another extended body, neither would be prior by nature. Each would have to be both cause and effect, leading to an unending series of bodies. But dimensions cannot extend without limit. — س قده

“Nature” here means either a kind essence or real existence. If a quantitative part were necessary in itself, it would still be only potential as a part, since a part of magnitude exists only as divisible magnitude. That conflicts with being necessary in itself. The clearer proof is the earlier argument that God, as Necessary Being, cannot have any limiting boundary.
This and the following proofs rule out every kind of part, not only parts of size. — ط مد ظله

The dependence here is dependence for existence, not just dependence in the way parts support a whole. Even if the composite whole were called necessary, the possible part’s existence would depend on the other Necessary Being; since existence is prior to essence, the whole would depend on that being for its existence. That contradicts the premise.

You might object that many wholes are made of parts that are not themselves the whole: a human being is made of animal and rational, and a house of roof and walls. But in a definition such as “animal, rational,” the parts are naturally related to the whole; a house is made of material of the same kind as its parts. The case of necessary and possible is different: the aspects of being free of nonexistence and being open to nonexistence have no such shared nature. — س قده
The same objection can be raised here—that a whole depends on its parts while a possible thing depends on God for existence. The reply is the same as in the previous note. — س قده

First, if something simple in thought were made of matter and form in reality, it would also have broader kind and defining feature in thought, which contradicts its supposed simplicity. Second, a thing simple in reality need not be simple in thought: accidents, for example, can be analyzed into broader kind and defining feature. This distinction preserves the two directions of the argument: simplicity in thought rules out external matter and form, though external simplicity alone does not rule out mental parts. — س قده

The broader kind depends on defining feature to become a definite kind of being, whether in the higher intellectual realm or in our own thought. In the material world, things also need features that place them in a class and make them individuals. A broader kind is incomplete and vague; it has no separate “lord” or ruler of its own, and cannot be pointed to in thought as a complete thing.

Predication requires unity in existence and multiplicity in meaning. If the parts were pure existence, there would be no distinct meanings to predicate. If they were essences other than existence, there would be distinct meanings but no common existence in which they could be one. If they were a mixture, one aspect would be only unity and the other only difference; neither would allow the required predication. Ordinary broader kind and defining feature can be predicated because they have a separate, accidental existence in the mind. But God’s essence is pure existence, not a mixture of existence and essence. — س قده

“Dividing defining feature” includes a feature that classifies a species, a subclass, or an individual. The phrase covers the possible divisions of essence: a composite species such as human, a simple species such as prime matter, or a most general kind. — س قده
The simple species is mentioned to cover every possibility. In essences, it has no broader kind above it and no species beneath it.

The previous proof began by denying essence and its dividing features. This proof begins from the fact that the Necessary Being is the highest degree of existence, so He cannot be indeterminate and await a feature that makes Him definite. — ط مد ظله

The phrase “becomes definite as an existent” applies to both kinds of feature. A species does not need a classifying feature to be pointed to by the mind; the reference may instead be to the inner senses that imagine or remember particular instances. — س قده
“Nature” here means nature as realized in individual things. No one would think that the bare nature itself—the subject of a general proposition—is divided into individuals.

True oneness is when a thing is one in itself, with no second feature serving as the basis of its unity. Non-true oneness applies when several things count as one because they share something: Zayd and ʿAmr are both human, while horses and cows are both animals. Humanity and animality are true unities; the people or animals that share them are one only in this derived sense. True unity may itself be the Necessary Being's self-subsisting oneness, or a unity added to a possible essence.

To be fair, the thinkers who offer these examples mean us to attend to the ways they bring the subject closer, not to the ways in which the comparison fails. Consider the soul and the body. God is above all literal comparisons, but the example can still teach us something. The body lives through the soul, which sustains it and is its inward life, although the soul is not simply a thing located inside the body or standing outside it. In a far higher way, the world lives through God's sustaining presence. He is the source that holds together every life and every bodily form. He does not enter things as a body enters a space, nor is He outside them as one separate object is outside another.

As the verse says, “In every thing there is a sign pointing to His oneness.” The highest examples can therefore reveal God's light and show how everything depends on the One. Seen in that way, all faces bow before the Living, the Sustainer. A thing, considered as a sign or face of its source, reveals that source through its own existence. God shows Himself through Himself and remains unlike what He creates.

We must not carry over the ways in which the human soul differs from God. The soul needs the body in certain respects, is affected by it, and comes to be with it. None of those features belongs to God. For that reason, after using an example, some writers immediately correct themselves and pray, as the Persian verse puts it: “You are beyond all that I can imagine or say; dust upon my head and upon my comparison!”

Still, the right response is not to ban all examples. Prophets used them, and the Qur'an does too, as in the verse that begins “The likeness of His light is as a niche.” There is a reason for this. Our minds, tied as they are to imagination, struggle to grasp meanings without giving them a picture. This reflects the correspondences between the levels of existence. When the intellect says that God is light—meaning an ever-living reality that exists through itself—the imagination pictures a dazzling ray. When it hears that He encompasses all things, it pictures a vast physical space. When it hears that He is above every other light, it pictures something literally higher, or the sun outshining the stars in daylight.

A mind trained in careful proof need not accept these pictures as literal truths. It can reject the imagination's mistake while keeping the meaning that the example was meant to suggest. It knows that God's attributes are far beyond bodily pictures. But consider the person whose thought is still ruled by imagination. Such a person's pictures may be as confused as dreams, whereas the images used by disciplined reason and spiritual insight can be like truthful dreams: they invite us to move from the picture to the reality it points toward.

If imagination were denied any examples, and the mind were given only abstract meanings, the two powers would quarrel. Imagination would refuse to follow reason. It would be like inviting guests to a table and feeding only some of them, though all need food. This may help explain the poet Rumi's saying that the images by which God's friends are drawn onward are reflections of the beautiful faces in God's garden. — س قده

The author himself is cautious about the analogy: the soul's relation to its body is not the same as a shopkeeper's relation to a shop. The analogy is limited and does not make the two relations identical.

The proof can be put briefly: anything from which some feature can be denied is made definite through both an affirmation and a negation. Whatever is formed from affirmation and negation is composite. By contraposition, what is simple in reality has nothing denied of it; it is all things. This is not ordinary predication, as in “Zayd is human” or “Zayd is standing.” Ordinary predicates include both their positive and negative boundaries, which would make a simple subject composite. Here, only the positive, existing perfections of things are present in the simple reality; it has every perfection and rules over every perfection. — ط مد ظله

To say that the perfectly simple reality “is all existences” is to give the reason in the description itself: it includes every perfection because it is simple. It is existence through and through, unmixed with any separate essence or absence. The word “as” in the passage means “because,” much as in the Qur'anic instruction to remember God because He has guided you.

The point is many perfections within one reality. One level of existence, through its undivided reality, contains the perfections found across all other existences. It can do, in its one reality, what the many do in their different ways. The statement does not mean one reality spread among many things, as some readers mistakenly suppose. They hear that the simple reality is “all things” and object that stones and clay would then have to be Necessary Being. That turns the claim around. It is not saying that every particular thing is the perfectly simple reality.

The spread of unity across the many belongs instead to God's all-embracing gift of existence, received by each thing according to its capacity. Spiritual writers have often described this second view. The first view—seeing all perfections gathered in divine simplicity—is the one the author regards as especially his own. He finds only a brief anticipation in Aristotle and says elsewhere that he has not found anyone who fully knows it.

Yet writers on spiritual knowledge also speak of seeing the many within the one and the one within the many. Perhaps the author means that they have not made the same distinction rigorously. We should not assume that their language means something crude when other, clearer statements in their works may explain it. A verse of ʿAṭṭār's Conference of the Birds seems to hint at the point: all are before Him, yet He precedes all; all are seen through Him, and He is seen through all.

Mīr Dāmād also writes that God is all existence and entirely existence, all beauty and perfection and entirely beauty and perfection; everything else is a flash of His light, a trace of His existence, and a shadow of His reality. This may mean that everything called “existent” gets that description from Him, whether we speak of His own existence or that of others. But that alone is not the complete claim at issue. The fuller argument and the careful closing of its difficulties remain, in this commentator's judgment, the author's achievement. — س قده

The “not being” that contributes to composition is not a separate existing thing. The deepest composition is a positive feature together with the denial of some perfection. Existence and existence are not two different kinds; the second aspect is absence, possibility, or a boundary. Even “impossible existence” has a kind of conceptual thinghood while remaining nonexistent. A possible thing likewise combines its essence, which is not itself existence, with the absence of other perfections. The word “Zayd” points to his existence, essence, and the perfections he lacks. Pure existence has no such lack or essence and is therefore not composite. — س قده

We are speaking about what exists in reality, not simply about an idea formed in the mind, although the author's wording might suggest otherwise. The Necessary Being has no foundation but pure existence. Lower levels of existence are different: what makes them the particular levels they are includes their limits, lacks, and absences.

Someone may object that we cannot say lower existences are made up of existence and nonexistence, since whatever actually exists is still an instance of existence. That objection confuses unrestricted reality with its limited levels. What makes a limited being this particular being is not another positive existence added alongside existence. Its limitation is real as a boundary, not as an independent thing.

Our honored teacher offers a simpler route to the result: God possesses every perfection found in anything else, and none of those perfections can be denied of Him. Necessary existence means that His existence cannot fail under any condition. Were it bounded, existence would be absent beyond the boundary, and so He would not be necessary without qualification. He must therefore be unrestricted. No way of existing, and no perfection belonging to existence, can be excluded from Him.

The same point appears in the first journey: negating “horse” of “human” is not pure nothingness, but a denial made of an existing subject. This answers the objection that a negative statement has no subject and therefore no aspect that could be compared with its positive aspect. In this context, a negative statement with an existing subject functions like an affirmative statement whose predicate is itself negated. — س قده

The immediate point is clear, but elsewhere in The Four Journeys and in The Witnesses the wording reads differently: “What makes a thing what it is differs from what makes it true to say that it is not another thing.” The conclusion does not follow plainly from that wording. The question is why a human being is not a horse, not why a human being is not human.

The author explains the point in The Secrets of the Verses. The meaning of a negative statement cannot be exactly the same as the meaning of a positive one, even when each is said in relation to something else. What the statement refers to is distinct from the meaning of the relation itself. Restricting a statement by that reference does not change the underlying nature of affirmation or denial. If the affirmation of A meant exactly the denial of B, affirmation itself would become denial. A thing would not be itself, which is impossible.

Put another way, suppose we deny the existence of ʿAmr of Zayd. If Zayd's own existence, considered together with its limits and lacks, were itself what made that denial true, it would be a combination of positive existence and absence. That is impossible in the case now being discussed. But if we denied ʿAmr's existence of Zayd's existence simply as existence, we would be making a thing other than itself: for in this argument we are considering existence as existence, not as one limited share of it. If it were only a particular share that was absent, the denial would rest on that share's limitation; that is the first case again. — س قده

“Unrestricted existence” and “restricted existence” here anticipate the mystics' terminology below. A kind's definition limits it to a narrow range of perfections; a possible essence is likewise a bounded mode of existence. If one existence included the perfections of a human being and a celestial being, it would not be the restricted kind “human.” — س قده

“A fully realized kind” means a kind complete in existence, not merely a concept with a complete definition. “Animal” is conceptually definable but remains an open, broader kind; further perfections can be added without losing the name.

Philosophers usually use “unrestricted” and “restricted” for mental concepts. Mystics use the terms for real existence itself, in the sense of a reality that has breadth and encompasses its manifestations. In this usage, the mystics' unrestricted existence is like the philosophers' “simple existence, which is all existences.” — س قده

This explanation begins from the fact that the unrestricted is the source of the restricted and contains the perfections of its effects. The earlier approach is, however, more far-reaching, for it also establishes true unity and other important conclusions. — ط مد ظله

The author gives another form of the argument. Rather than begin with “the simple is all existences,” begin with the claim that the source and final end of all existence is their perfection. A giver of good cannot lack the good it gives, and a thing's end is its own perfection. If the end lacked that perfection, reaching it would not be completion but a change into something else.

A long line loses no part of line itself when separated into shorter lengths; it loses only endpoints and points of division. Those limits are not lines, and points are a different kind of thing from lines. — س قده

The verse about water more directly illustrates unity spread through multiplicity than multiplicity within unity. “Living” is explanatory here, not restrictive: every thing has life and awareness in its own way. — س قده

The flow of existence through things does not mean that the divine source acquires the changing attributes of what it flows through. In this sense, its light shines through every reality, and nothing veils it except its own majesty.

Every thing glorifies God through His own praise: all existents reveal His names and attributes. Their praise is not merely evidence of a maker, as theologians often say; every good and beautiful existence belongs first to God and only then to a thing's particular form. The editor connects this with the saying, “I have not seen a thing without seeing God before it.” The Qur'an speaks both of creatures praising and of God praising Himself. “Understanding their praise” means awareness that they are aware; embodied people cannot attain this knowledge of knowledge unless they are freed from bodily veils. — س قده

The two examples point to a distinction between an attribute that is purely real and one that is real but necessarily involves a relation. Attributes, whether used of God or created beings, fall into four kinds.

First are negative attributes: statements that deny something. Even a word without an obvious “not,” such as blindness or inability to read, can express the absence of sight or learning. With God, an example is holiness, understood as freedom from defect. Second are purely relational attributes, such as being the knower of an object or having power over it, when we mean only the relation itself. Third are real attributes that involve no relation and do not require one, such as life, necessary existence through oneself, or a knower's awareness of itself. Fourth are real attributes which are not relations in themselves but necessarily involve one, such as knowledge of another thing or power over it. Zayd's knowledge of the sun, for example, is a form or quality in his mind. It is not itself the relation between Zayd and the external sun, but it gives rise to that relation: he is the knower of the sun.

We can now see why negative attributes are not identical with the essence of the one described. Otherwise the subject would itself be an absence. Someone may reply that the reality to which a negative description applies can still be the divine essence, just as God's real positive attributes are identical with it even though their meanings differ. But absence and negation have no independently existing instance. An existent thing cannot itself be an instance of nonexistence. It can only be the reality from which our mind draws a negative statement. A positive meaning, by contrast, can be truly realized in something that exists. And a general nature can exist through the individual that genuinely realizes it.

Another objection is that God's negative attributes often deny a negation and therefore affirm something. The answer is that negation, considered simply as negation, still has no positive reality corresponding to it. Any positive force in the double negation comes from the existing thing that makes the statement true, not from negation as such.

Purely relational attributes are likewise not additional parts of the essence. If they were identical with it as relations, the subject would be nothing but a relation. The same question and answer apply: a real being allows us to describe a relation, but the relation considered as a concept is not the being itself.

How, then, can a negation or a relation count as an attribute at all? Because the mind does not require every true description to be a separate object existing outside it. The description must be grounded in how matters really stand. For example, “being a universal kind” can truly be said of human beings or horses even though universality is something the mind recognises rather than a physical part of either animal. Thus the real, positive attributes of God, both purely real attributes and those that imply relations, are identical with His essence. The negative and merely relational descriptions are not additional realities in Him. — س قده

Here the author means the concept of God's sustaining relation, under which all His particular relations to things can be gathered. God's true existence sustains unrestricted existence, which some call the all-embracing mercy. Unrestricted existence, in turn, sustains limited beings in a dependent way. Besides these realities, we can speak of relational sustaining power: an idea that gathers all the relations philosophers say are additional to the divine essence.

Could the author's meaning be different? Perhaps the realities from which we draw these relational attributes all return to the true, life-giving relation just described. On that reading, they are its aspects, and it contains them as the many divine names and attributes are understood to be contained within divine oneness. Each name would be the one named, considered through a particular perfection, as the mystics teach.

But this reading does not fit what the author says a few lines later: these relational attributes come after both the one related and the things related to Him. The true sustaining power does not come after what it sustains. It belongs to the very first level of reality and precedes everything through that precedence. Indeed, as the act of connecting one thing with another, it cannot simply be judged identical with the essence or an additional part of it in the way an ordinary attribute can.

Finally, the sustaining relation spoken of as an attribute means giving and upholding existence. If we instead take “self-sustaining” to mean only standing through oneself, it would no longer be a relational attribute in the sense used here. — س قده
God's sustaining relation means that every other being, and every existing aspect of it, depends on Him for its existence.

The author's qualification concerns denying positive existence, not denying absences or deficiencies. Denials of lack do not multiply aspects in God; denials of one real perfection from another being do. — ط مد ظله

Avicenna's statement can be read as saying not that no negations multiply, but that not every negation multiplies. Denying a perfection may multiply aspects in what is described; denying a deficiency does not. Even if the sentence is read as a universal denial, it can mean that negations do not multiply in themselves, since nothing distinguishes absences as absences; any multiplicity lies in what is denied. The author, however, rejects the claim that such negations have no effect on the subject at all.

“Extended” refers to the body's spatial form, which is sometimes loosely called “body” because it is what first appears to the senses. In a composite body, extension is only one part, not the whole body. — س قده

This follows the Illuminationist view that intellects are pure existence without essences. Or it may mean an intellect's knowledge of itself: knowledge is plainly additional to the bare concept of intellect, since no essence, considered by itself, is either knowing or ignorant. — س قده

The apparent circle is that God's life, knowledge, power, and will are said to depend on His essence, while His essence is said to depend on these attributes for its perfection. The answer is that God's living, knowing, powerful essence is already presupposed; otherwise, the attributes could not arise from it. There is no dependence on an external thing. — س قده

God's essence is the source of the attributes, while the attributes are perfections of the essence. The objection makes the essence seem more perfect than itself by comparing it with what proceeds from it, and then comparing it with what perfects it.

Al-Farabi extends the usual proof of necessary existence to every perfection: if knowledge is not necessary in itself, it depends on another, which must itself be knowing, since a giver of perfection cannot lack it. Continue this reasoning until reaching knowledge that exists through itself. The same applies to power, will, and other perfections. — س قده

A perfection is not a mere absence, such as an essence or a thing's bare existence. Whatever is drawn from existence precisely as existence must be identical with existence, not something added to it. Since the Necessary Being is pure, affirmative existence, every perfection drawn from existence belongs to Him through His essence.

In their first approach, later thinkers missed the reality of existence and treated the attributes' identity as a sameness of concepts. In their second approach, which said that the same effects follow from God's essence as follow from the attributes, they missed the degrees of real existence. — س قده

Even if the later thinkers' proof succeeds, it shows only that God has no attribute distinct from His essence. That is not yet the same as proving that all His attributes are identical with His essence.
The argument assumes that an attribute is something different from the thing it describes. Without that assumption, the claim that it depends on a subject would need to be proved. — ط مد ظله

A created thing cannot be the source of God's attribute, since the effect depends on God, and the attributes through which God acts—knowledge, will, and power—are already required for its creation. That would produce a circle. The gravest dependence would be for God to depend on an effect of His own. — س قده
“May” here means “sometimes”: it is enough to show that an agent can act on something else. A universal claim would beg the question and would not follow from the proof. — س قده

If acting and receiving were one and the same aspect, then whatever acts in a given respect would also receive in that same respect, and vice versa. Prime matter receives but does not act; a substantial form acts but does not receive its own effect. The point is not that a thing can never both act and receive in different respects. — س قده

Another possibility is that one aspect is identical with God's essence and the other is a necessary consequence of it. The author does not mention this option, perhaps because it leads even more clearly to a problem. If the essential aspect gives rise to the other, the two relations of acting and receiving would have to come from different aspects; otherwise they would conflict. If the second aspect came from yet another necessary consequence, the sequence would continue without end; if it ended in another essential aspect, God would be composite.

Receiving through passive change means gaining a fitting perfection through another thing, with matter playing a role; water receives heat in this way. Receiving in the broader sense simply means being described by something that necessarily belongs to a thing; fire is hot in this way. A simple nature considered apart from matter can still be characterized by its necessary qualities. The aspect through which it has these qualities is the same as the aspect from which they follow. — س قده

This is a further point, not a conclusion of the preceding argument. If the attributes are necessary consequences of God's essence, they do not need a separate act that makes them exist; their existence follows the essence. — س قده

The proof assumes that any attribute depends on a subject in which it inheres. That does not apply to relational attributes, which are concepts the mind draws from relations and do not inhere in God as added qualities.

There is a problem with this claim. It describes an animal's power, not God's. God's power means that the act follows His knowledge and will. The author has explained this in his other books. Al-Khafrī was wrong to claim that two meanings of power must always go together: being able to produce an act, and being such that one acts if one wills and does not act if one does not will. I think this objection, and several of the objections before and after it apart from the first, come from later thinkers. The author reports them without naming their sources and does not answer them here because he has already settled the question elsewhere. He also says that he will return to it. Notice that he opens the first discussion with 'We say' and introduces his own later conclusions with 'I say.' This suggests that the disputes between those passages are reports of arguments from later scholars. — س قده

This objection distinguishes existence in itself from existence as an attribute in another thing, treating them as different kinds of existence. The reply that follows instead treats them as one reality and identity, with different external relations. — س قده

“The first” refers to the objection that an effect is necessary in itself but possible in its receiver. “The second” refers to the claim that the receiver does not undo the necessity given by the agent.

The reply is that the effect's existence in a receiver also depends on an agent. Its existence in itself is likewise possible and depends on a cause; in this way, both kinds of existence are connected to both necessity and possibility.

The point is not a technical side issue in the debate. The objector has denied a premise of the argument, so the author must establish that premise itself. He does so in a way that answers the objection rather than merely attacking a narrower supporting point.

The proof seems to assume what its opponent already accepts: that God's essence is not itself knowledge or power, even if those attributes always accompany it. The missing premise is that an essence entirely bare of these perfections and their opposites would have to be a defined essence, not pure existence. — س قده

The proof rests on three claims: God has attributes such as knowledge, power, and life; these are perfections; and a giver cannot lack what it gives. The first is established later, the second is self-evident, and the third is argued in the discussion of cause and effect. — ط مد ظله

If the attributes are necessary consequences of God's essence, He does not gain perfection from them; they always follow from Him and come from Him. The stronger point is that an essence lacking both the perfections and their opposites would involve a real potentiality to receive them. Real potentiality requires matter, which would make God bodily. — س قده

Even those who say essences are fundamentally real still treat an essence as conceptual when it is considered apart from its actual existence. Its necessary consequences are conceptual in the same way.

The attributes cannot flow from an essence that lacks them, because a giver of perfection must possess it; nor can they flow from an essence already identical with the highest attributes, because that would assume the point being proved. The argument would require a higher aspect in God, which is impossible.

This is a consequence of the proof, not the proof's direct conclusion. The argument establishes that God is existence, knowledge, power, life, and every perfection in Himself. It does not by itself establish that each exists on its own and that all are one. The consequence can also be turned into a separate proof of identity. — ط مد ظله
